title: Separating and analysing - 123 school
heading: Separating and analysing
intro: These questions are about separation methods, chromatography, the Rf value, the calibration line and titration.
Test your knowledge by typing your answer and comparing it with the correct answer. Then click 'Check answers'.

questions.q: What is a mixture?
questions.a: A product that consists of more than one pure substance

questions.q: What difference is filtration based on?
questions.a: The difference in particle size: the solid particles stay behind on the filter, the liquid passes through

questions.q: What difference is distillation based on?
questions.a: The difference in boiling point: the substance with the lowest boiling point evaporates first

questions.q: You want to get the salt out of salt water. Which separation method do you use?
questions.a: Evaporation: the water evaporates and the salt remains

questions.q: What is the difference between evaporation and distillation?
questions.a: With evaporation the evaporated substance is lost, with distillation the vapour is condensed again and collected

questions.q: What difference is extraction based on?
questions.a: The difference in solubility: a substance dissolves better in one solvent than in another

questions.q: What difference is settling (sedimentation) based on?
questions.a: The difference in density: the heavier particles sink to the bottom

questions.q: What is decanting?
questions.a: Carefully pouring off the liquid above the settled solid

questions.q: What does a centrifuge do?
questions.a: It spins a mixture quickly so that the heavier particles move to the bottom faster

questions.q: What is adsorption?
questions.a: The attachment of particles to the surface of a solid, for example dyes to activated carbon

questions.q: How do you separate iron filings from sand?
questions.a: With a magnet, because iron is magnetic and sand is not

questions.q: Name three separation methods
questions.a: For example filtration, distillation, evaporation, extraction, settling, adsorption or chromatography

questions.q: What do you use chromatography for?
questions.a: To separate the substances in a mixture and to recognise them

questions.q: What are the mobile and the stationary phase in chromatography?
questions.a: The mobile phase is the solvent that moves up along the paper; the stationary phase is the paper (or other material) that stays in place

questions.q: What difference is chromatography based on?
questions.a: The difference in how strongly the substances attach to the stationary phase and how well they dissolve in the mobile phase

questions.q: Why must the starting line in paper chromatography be above the layer of solvent?
questions.a: Otherwise the spots dissolve in the liquid in the container and do not travel up the paper

questions.q: In which BINAS table is information about chromatography found?
questions.a: Table 37F

questions.q: How do you calculate the Rf value of a substance?
questions.a: Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent (both measured from the starting line)

questions.q: Can the Rf value be larger than 1? Explain
questions.a: No, because a substance cannot travel further than the solvent

questions.q: A substance travels 3.0 cm, the solvent 6.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value
A substance has Rf = 0.40. The solvent has travelled 10.0 cm. How far has the substance travelled?
How do you recognise with chromatography whether two substances are the same?
questions.a: Under the same conditions they travel the same distance (same Rf value), so they end up at the same height

questions.q: On a chromatogram an unknown mixture shows two spots. What do you conclude?
questions.a: The mixture contains at least two different substances

questions.q: What is the retention time in gas chromatography?
questions.a: The time a substance needs to travel through the column; under the same conditions it is always the same for a given substance, so you can use it to recognise substances

questions.q: What is a calibration line?
questions.a: A graph of a measured value (for example absorbance) against the concentration, made with solutions of known concentration

questions.q: What do you use a calibration line for?
questions.a: To read the concentration from the measured value of an unknown solution

questions.q: How do you use a calibration line to find an unknown concentration?
questions.a: Measure the value of the unknown solution, find that value on the vertical axis, go across to the line and read the concentration from the horizontal axis

questions.q: What is titration?
questions.a: Adding a solution of known concentration to a measured amount of another solution until the reaction is exactly complete

questions.q: In a titration the burette reading at the start is 12.45 mL and at the end 24.72 mL. How many mL was added?
What do you use an indicator for in a titration?
questions.a: To see from the colour change when the reaction is exactly complete

questions.q: How do you calculate the number of moles from a concentration and a volume?
questions.a: n = c × V (volume in litres, concentration in mol/L)

questions.q: 25.0 mL of HCl needs 20.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L NaOH (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O). Calculate the concentration of the HCl
Why do you repeat a titration several times and take the average?
questions.a: The result is more reliable, because measurement errors partly cancel out
